power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

text.text: proposed that lower-class contexts foster tighter norms and a broader preference for order over openness through greater exposure to socioeconomic threat and, in turn, heightened vigilance toward danger.
This account has potentially far-reaching implications.
We reanalyzed their publicly available data to evaluate the direction, generality, and mechanism of the class-tightness link.

Study 1 did not show greater lower-class support for specific punitive responses in the original ratings; class differences in the perceived appropriateness of norm violations and of doing nothing in response were no longer significant after response-set adjustment.
Total associations in Studies 3 and 4 were mostly nonsignificant or opposite to the proposed lower-class-tightness pattern, despite significant threat-related indirect effects.
Word-embedding analyses generally supported a Class × Tightness-Looseness interaction, but no model reproduced two significant simple effects in the predicted directions.

Study 2 yielded average associations consistent with the predicted lower-class preference for order over openness, but substantial heterogeneity and prediction intervals spanning zero left the generality of this pattern unresolved.

In Study 5, assignment to the lower-class Bimboola condition produced higher scores on both tightness measures, but neither indirect effect through the preregistered mediator, perceived socioeconomic threat, was significant.

Together, our reanalyses support some associations between social class and norm-related outcomes, but they do not establish the proposed general lower-classtightness pattern or its threat-based mechanism.
These findings call for a more differentiated account of how specific features of class contexts relate to cultural tightness-looseness.

Social norms are pervasive in human societies, yet groups vary in norm strength and tolerance of deviance-a dimension known as cultural tightness-looseness (Gelfand et al., 2006 (Gelfand et al., , 2011)). Lin et al. (2026) extended this framework to social class, proposing that social class is not merely a marker of socioeconomic standing but a form of within-society cultural ecology.

These class-based differences in norm strength were further expected to extend to a broader orderopenness trade-off.

The class-tightness link was theorized to operate through a threat-based pathway in which lower-class contexts expose individuals to greater socioeconomic threat, heightening vigilance toward danger and thereby promoting the experience, endorsement, and socialization of tight norms. text.text: This account is consequential.

It could help explain class-linked differences in norm adherence, tolerance of deviance, and support for punishment, as well as how such differences may contribute to the persistence of social inequality (Lin et al., 2026).

text.text: It could also inform more responsive institutional policies and practices for lower-class individuals.
These implications depend, however, on how consistently the predicted class-tightness pattern is observed and how well the proposed threat pathway is supported.

text.text: Across Studies 1, 3, and 4, as well as the supplemental word-embedding analysis, the evidence did not consistently support the predicted lower-class-tightness pattern.

Study 2 yielded average associations consistent with the hypothesized lower-class preference for order over openness, but substantial heterogeneity and prediction intervals spanning zero left the generality of this pattern unresolved.

Our reanalyses of Supplemental Study 1, a diary study, supported the reported associations of lower social class with greater punishment motivation and a higher likelihood of self-reported punishment.

However, our reanalyses also identified ambiguity in the interpretation of sanction support in Study 1, sensitivity of its focal results to respondentlevel adjustment, mostly nonsignificant or opposite-direction total associations between social-class indicators and tightness outcomes in Studies 3 and 4, and limited support for the full predicted pattern in the word-embedding analyses.

text.text: Using GloVe Common Crawl embeddings, they computed pairwise cosine similarities between higher-and lower-class words and tightness-looseness words and tested whether these similarities varied by class, tightness-looseness, and their interaction.

Their analysis yielded a significant Class × Tightness-Looseness interaction and two significant simple effects in the predicted directions, with tightness words more similar to lower-class than to higher-class words and looseness words showing the reverse pattern.
They interpreted these findings as evidence that collective semantic representations link lower social class to tighter norms and higher social class to looser norms.
We re-estimated the interaction and simple-effect models after addressing two issues in Lin et al.'s (2026) original GloVe analysis.

text.text: First, the released dataset contained 4,120 rows, whereas Lin et al.'s reported word lists imply 4,080 word pairs [(51 higher-class words + 51 lower-class words) × (20 tightness words + 20 looseness words)].
The additional 40 rows resulted from duplicate pairings involving the lower-class word "impoverished."

Second, the original simple-effect models did not fully account for the crossed structure of the data, in which each social-class word was paired with multiple tightness-looseness words, and each tightness-looseness word was paired with multiple social-class words.

Lin et al.'s simpleeffect models included a random intercept only for tightness-looseness words, whereas their interaction model accounted for this crossed structure by including random intercepts for both word sets.
We therefore removed the 40 additional rows and fitted each simple-effect model with crossed random intercepts for both social-class and tightness-looseness words.
After these corrections, the Class × Tightness-Looseness interaction remained significant, B = 0.039, SE = 0.005, p < .001.

Looseness words were not significantly more similar to higher-class than lower-class words, B = -0.016, SE = 0.014, p = .256.
Both simple-effect coefficients represent lower-class minus higher-class cosine similarity.
Although both simple-effect estimates were in the predicted directions, neither was significant.
Thus, the corrected analysis supports a relative contrast but does not establish the two directional class differences that constitute the full predicted pattern.
The full predicted pattern was also not reproduced across alternative embedding models.

text.text: A "Fundamental Class Divergence" in Order Versus Openness?

Lin et al.'s (2026) second hypothesis extended their tightness-looseness account to a broader divergence in preferences, with lower-class individuals favoring order more and openness less than higher-class individuals.

text.text: Study 2 examined this hypothesis through a meta-analysis of correlations derived from national and cross-national survey databases spanning 52 years and 140 countries.
The analyses covered 175 survey items grouped into 10 topics.

The authors reported that both current social class (respondents' socioeconomic position at the time of the survey) and class origin (their socioeconomic background during upbringing) were negatively associated, on average, with preferences for order over openness.
They interpreted these findings as identifying a "fundamental class divergence in order versus openness" (p. 10).
Our reanalyses revealed substantial heterogeneity and prediction intervals spanning zero, both overall and within most topics, raising questions about the generality of the proposed class difference.

The 10 topics were conventionalism, need for structure, tight values, morality, support for punishment, law and governance, experiences of freedom versus constraint, gender attitudes, ethnocentrism, and prejudice (Lin et al., 2026).

text.text: Extending the account across these diverse topics required judgments about which survey items represented order versus openness and how they should be grouped.

For example, similarly worded questions about attitudes toward having immigrants or foreign workers as neighbors were assigned to the ethnocentrism topic in Afrobarometer and the prejudice topic in the World Values Survey/European Values Study (their Supplemental Table S13). text.text: We transformed the correlations to Fisher's z and fitted separate multilevel meta-analytic models for current social class and class origin.
The models incorporated sampling variances and random intercepts for database-specific items, countries, and survey waves.
This cross-classified structure modeled clustering by shared items and survey contexts (Fernández-Castilla et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This cross-classified structure modeled clustering by shared items and survey contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Fernández-Castilla et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In our models, the pooled associations were negative for both current social class and class origin (Fisher's zs = -0.074 and -0.132, respectively), but the associations contributing to these averages varied substantially.
We quantified this variation using I², which estimates the proportion of variation in effect estimates attributable to heterogeneity rather than sampling error (Higgins et al., 2003).

text.text: For the multilevel models, total I² was calculated using the sum of the estimated item-, country-, and survey-wave-level heterogeneity variances and the typical sampling variance (Cheung, 2014).

text.text: The resulting estimates were 90.6% for current social class and 88.2% for class origin, both indicating high heterogeneity.
Under the fitted models, approximately nine tenths of the total variation in effect estimates was attributable to differences in the underlying associations rather than sampling error.
Assessing the generality of the proposed class difference therefore requires examining the range of associations underlying these negative averages.
The pooled means and their confidence intervals describe the average associations and uncertainty about those averages, rather than the spread of the underlying associations (Deeks et al., 2024).

text.text: We therefore calculated 95% prediction intervals to characterize the range of underlying associations.

These intervals incorporate heterogeneity as well as uncertainty about the pooled mean, providing a model-based range for the true association in a comparable combination of survey item, country, and wave (Riley et al., 2011).

text.text: Both overall prediction intervals crossed zero: [-0.239, 0.091] for current social class and [-0.271, 0.006] for class origin, on Fisher's z scale.
Despite the negative pooled means, these ranges encompassed an absence of the hypothesized class difference for comparable item-setting combinations.
The uncertainty therefore concerned whether the class difference would be present for particular measures and settings, as well as how strong it would be.

Heterogeneity remained substantial within topics, with total I² ranging from 87.0% to 98.3% for current social class and from 80.2% to 97.4% for class origin.

The heterogeneity was therefore not confined to differences between topics.

Adding tightness accounted for little of the total heterogeneity, and prediction intervals at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of country-level tightness included zero for both class indicators (Supplemental Table S7).

text.text: Is the Threat-Based Mechanism Established?

Lin et al.'s (2026) third claim was that class-based differences in tightness-looseness arise because lower-class contexts expose individuals to greater socioeconomic threat, which heightens perceptions of danger and, in turn, promotes the experience, endorsement, and socialization of tighter norms.

text.text: Studies 3 and 4 reported indirect associations consistent with this account, with socioeconomic threat followed by perceived danger (Study 3) or danger vigilance (Study 4) as sequential mediators.

These cross-sectional mediation analyses, however, do not establish the proposed causal sequence (MacKinnon et al., 2007), a limitation that Lin et al. (2026) acknowledged when discussing Study 3 in their supplemental materials (p. 30).

text.text: The pattern of total and direct associations further qualifies the interpretation of these indirect effects.
As shown above, total associations in Studies 3 and 4 did not consistently follow the proposed lower-class-tightness pattern.
We also examined Lin et al.'s (2026) publicly released mediation-model outputs for current social class and class origin, summarized in our Supplemental Table S8.

text.text: In seven of the nine models, both the serial and total indirect effects were significantly negative, whereas the direct effects were significantly positive.
This pattern is commonly described as inconsistent or competitive mediation (MacKinnon et al., 2000; Zhao et al., 2010).

text.text: In those seven models, the negative total indirect effects were offset by positive direct effects, leaving total associations that were either nonsignificant or significantly positive.
These indirect effects therefore do not, on their own, establish that socioeconomic threat explains a general lower-class-tightness pattern.
In Study 5, Lin et al. (2026) tested the class-tightness link experimentally using an adapted Bimboola paradigm that jointly varied class position and threat-related socioecological conditions.

text.text: The conditions differed in assigned group income, job eligibility, housing affordability, neighborhood crime, and grocery constraints.

Participants in the lowerclass condition rated tightness-related behaviors as more important (importance of tightness) and perceived stronger norms in their hypothetical Bimboola environment (tightness in life) than those in the higher-class condition. Lin et al. (2026) interpreted these differences as a coping response to socioeconomic threat.

text.text: The condition effects, however, do not establish that perceived socioeconomic threat accounted for the differences in tightness.
Their Study 5 preregistration (Question 8) explicitly proposed testing whether perceived socioeconomic threat, assessed using the manipulation check, mediated the condition effects.
This mediation analysis was not reported in the article or supplemental materials and was not included in the released Study 5 analysis code.
We therefore tested this hypothesis using the publicly available data.
The two manipulation-check items asked participants to rate their assigned group on response scales ranging from financially insecure to financially abundant and from poor to rich.
We used the two-item composite provided in the released data and reverse-scored it so that higher scores represented greater perceived socioeconomic threat.
Experimental condition was coded 1 for the lower-class condition and 0 for the higher-class condition.
The mediator composite and both outcome scores were standardized before model estimation.

We fitted separate single-mediator models for importance of tightness and tightness in life, using 5,000 bootstrap resamples to estimate 95% percentile confidence intervals for the indirect effects (MacKinnon et al., 2007; Shrout & Bolger, 2002).

Neither indirect effect was significant: ab = -0.175, 95% CI [-0.517, 0.167], for importance of tightness, and ab = -0.035, 95% CI [-0.392, 0.320], for tightness in life.

Our mediation analyses of Study 5 did not support perceived socioeconomic threat as the process accounting for the experimental effects.

text.text: The inconsistent directions in our reanalyses undermine the empirical basis for that generalization.
Interpreting Study 2's overall and topic-specific averages as evidence of a broad class divide in order versus openness requires considering the variation among the associations they summarize.
Our reanalyses revealed substantial heterogeneity and prediction intervals that included zero, both overall and within most topics.
The uncertainty about generality therefore arose within the evidence selected to support the cultural divide, rather than only at unexamined boundaries of the account.
The proposed cultural account needs to address variation within topics and specify which class differences in preferences it explains and under what conditions.
The threat-based explanation requires evidence that socioeconomic threat accounts for the proposed class differences in tightness.
The cross-sectional mediation analyses in Studies 3 and 4 did not establish causal ordering.

Moreover, their negative indirect effects often coexisted with positive direct effects, so the threat-related paths did not, by themselves, characterize the overall direction of the class-tightness associations.
An adaptive account should connect specific features of socioeconomic disadvantage to the psychological processes through which they shape behavior (Sheehy-Skeffington, 2020).

Study 5 showed that the combined Bimboola manipulation affected tightness-related responses, but our mediation reanalysis did not support perceived socioeconomic threat as the process accounting for those effects.
The present evidence therefore leaves open which psychological processes link class contexts to normative responses.
Further theoretical development requires accounting for the variation in class-related normative responses and specifying when and why class differences in norm strength emerge.
A general contrast between tighter lower-class and looser higher-class cultures must be empirically established before it can serve as a premise for explaining the persistence of social inequality.
